title: The last Mughal, 1857
hookLine: the last Mughal emperor is exiled after the uprising in India

lines: AN EMPIRE ENDS ON A SHIP.
cards: An elderly emperor sits in the Red Fort in Delhi, writing poetry. He rules very little beyond its walls; the British East India Company holds the real power.

Then soldiers in the Company's own army rise up, march on Delhi, and call on him to lead them. He hesitates, then lends them his name. For a few months the old poet is again the center of an empire's hopes.
When the British retake the city, he is put on trial and sent far away, across the sea. A dynasty that ruled for generations ends with an old man on a ship. Today: the last Mughal.

teach.b: His name was Bahadur Shah, and he wrote under the pen name Zafar, which means victory. A man called victory, remembered for a defeat.
The Mughals had built the Taj Mahal and ruled much of South Asia; by Zafar's time, their power was mostly ceremony.
Then came the uprising the British called a mutiny, and that others in India later called a war of independence. Even the name is still argued over, and an honest telling says so.
The rising failed. Delhi was retaken, and the reprisals were brutal. Some of the emperor's sons were killed.
Zafar was tried, found guilty, and exiled to Rangoon, in what is now Myanmar, where he died far from home. Now the poet's part.
A couplet often attributed to him laments that the unlucky Zafar could not find even two yards of earth for his grave in the lane of the beloved. Scholars debate whether he wrote it.
People keep reciting it anyway, because it says what his life became: a king who couldn't choose his own grave. How does the Qur'an speak of endings like this?

teach.h: THERE REMAINETH BUT THE COUNTENANCE OF THY LORD.
teach.b: In surah ar-Rahman, in Pickthall's words: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." Every throne, every dynasty, every poet.
What lasts, the verse says, is not ours. The crown was taken. The ghazals he wrote are still sung.

how: Visitors still come to Bahadur Shah Zafar's tomb in Yangon to pray and to recite his poetry, and his ghazals are sung in Urdu across South Asia.

games.q: you're an old emperor with almost no real power. rebel soldiers arrive at your gates and ask you to lead them. what do you do?
o: hesitate, then lend them your name.
games.why: Zafar hesitated, then lent the rising his name. when it failed, he was tried and exiled.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that has ended or is ending: a job, a home, a friendship, a version of yourself. Don't fix it or argue with it; look at it like an old photograph, and notice what you carried out of it.
If you pray, you can say the words of Qur'an 55, that everyone passes and the Countenance of the Lord remains; if not, just breathe with what has ended.

wordCard.voice: Zafar. Victory, the pen name of Bahadur Shah, the last Mughal emperor, exiled after the rising, who died far from Delhi. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: victory, the pen name of the last Mughal emperor.

carryVoice: Your line: the last emperor. A crown can be taken while a song keeps going. Back tomorrow, same hill.
